euler_bubble.name: Shock Meets a Light Bubble
euler_bubble.question: How does the density contrast alter the interface deformation?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How does the density contrast alter the interface deformation?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A planar shock crosses a bubble of lighter gas. Misaligned pressure and density gradients deposit vorticity on the interface (the baroclinic torque) and roll the bubble into a vortex pair.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Open the Heavy Bubble scene (density ratio 3): the shock slows and focuses inside it instead.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The kinetic energy jump as the shock passes and the roll-up that follows.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
A shock wave moving through air meets a bubble of a different (here lighter) gas. Two things happen. First, the shock travels faster in the light gas, so it bends and focuses as it crosses the bubble. Second — and this is the key mechanism — the bubble's interface is a density gradient, while the shock is a pressure gradient, and where those two gradients are misaligned the equations generate vorticity. This is the baroclinic torque, ∝ ∇ρ × ∇p.

That deposited vorticity rolls the bubble up into a pair of counter-rotating vortices and stirs the two gases together. This shock-bubble interaction is the canonical model of the Richtmyer–Meshkov instability — the impulsive cousin of Rayleigh–Taylor — which controls mixing in supersonic combustion (scramjets) and is a central obstacle in inertial-confinement fusion, where it spoils the symmetry of the imploding fuel.

It is solved with exactly the same compressible Euler / HLLC machinery as the explosion; only the initial condition differs.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• U, F(U), ∂t U + ∇·F(U) = 0, γ — the compressible Euler conservation laws (see the Detonation exhibit)
• M_s — the shock Mach number you set; the post-shock density, pressure and velocity follow from the exact Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions, so a stronger shock means a hotter, faster, more compressed incoming flow
• ρ_bub/ρ_air — the bubble-to-air density ratio: below 1 the bubble is light (the shock speeds through and it rolls up fast), above 1 it is heavy (the shock focuses inside it); this ratio sets the sign and size of the baroclinic torque
• baroclinic vorticity generation, ∝ ∇ρ×∇p, is what rolls the bubble up

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: A planar incident shock travelling into still gas, set just upstream of a lighter (or heavier) gas bubble at rest; the twin-bubble variant seeds two.
layers.bc: The incident shock is set as an initial condition (a post-shock slab); all domain edges are zero-gradient (weakly reflecting) outflow; the bubble is a density contrast, not a wall, so the shock passes through and deforms it.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: Same compressible finite-volume scheme (MUSCL + minmod, HLLC Riemann solver, SSP-RK2, γ = 1.4). One or two circular bubbles of a chosen density ratio sit in still air; the incoming flow is the exact Rankine–Hugoniot post-shock state for the Mach number you set, so shock strength and density contrast are both physical, tunable inputs.
layers.checks: Qualitative demonstration: the same solver passes the Sod comparison; the classic experiments (Haas & Sturtevant 1987) are cylindrical/spherical and not reproduced quantitatively here.

layers.title: References
items: Haas, J.-F. & Sturtevant, B. (1987). Interaction of weak shock waves with cylindrical and spherical gas inhomogeneities. J. Fluid Mech. 181, 41–76.
Toro, E.F. (2009). Riemann Solvers and Numerical Methods for Fluid Dynamics, 3rd ed. Springer (HLLC, exact Sod solution).

euler_bubble_heavy.name: Shock Meets a Heavy Bubble
euler_bubble_heavy.question: What changes when the bubble is denser than the surrounding gas?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: What changes when the bubble is denser than the surrounding gas?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: The same shock hitting a bubble three times denser than the gas around it. The shock slows inside the bubble and the vorticity has the opposite sense, so the interface deforms differently.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Compare with the light bubble in the run history.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The direction of the roll-up and the slower interface response.
more: Try density ratio 1.0 as the null case.

euler_twin.name: Twin Bubbles
euler_twin.question: How do two shocked interfaces interact?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How do two shocked interfaces interact?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: Two stacked light bubbles struck by the same shock. Their roll-ups interact and tangle.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Compare with the single bubble at the same Mach number.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The interaction of the two vortex pairs.

target.label: Target
target.help: One gas bubble, or two stacked bubbles whose roll-ups interact.

mach.label: Shock Mach number
mach.help: Strength of the incoming shock, M_s = (shock speed)/(sound speed). The post-shock state follows the exact Rankine–Hugoniot relations (see derived quantities).

densratio.label: Density ratio ρ_bubble/ρ_air
densratio.help: Bubble density ÷ ambient density. <1 = a light bubble (rolls up fast); >1 = a heavy bubble (the shock slows and focuses inside it).

bubble.label: Bubble size
bubble.help: Bubble radius as a fraction of the domain height.

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
